decisions.question: Should repeated search words add weight?

branches.action: Use a set of normalized terms; membership is enough.

decisions.lead_in: Search ranking is the order in which matching documents are shown. A scoring rule assigns points to matches. Counting a repeated query word several times would add points several times, which is why the treatment of repetition has to be decided first.

problem.title: Why do repeated words change the results?
problem.problem: A user searches for “NOTICE notice!” and receives a different ranking than when searching for “notice”. For this product, repeating the same search term should not change its contribution. Decide which values should be treated as equivalent.
reasoning: For the query “LEASE lease!”, comparing the raw pieces would treat capitalization and punctuation as differences.
The supplied helper turns both pieces into “lease”. If repeated words should not affect ranking, keep a single “lease” in the query-term set.
Now compare that term with each document’s normalized title and body. Repeating it in the query no longer adds extra contributions.

strategy.name: Canonicalization before deduplication
strategy.mechanism: Convert equivalent representations into a shared form, then remove duplicates before counting contributions.
strategy.use_case: A search query repeats a term with different capitalization. The same pattern also appears when normalizing tags before aggregation or comparing imported identifiers under a defined normalization policy.
strategy.prompt: “Repeated or differently capitalized search words change ranking unexpectedly. What would you inspect?”
strategy.recognize: Should “LEASE” and “lease” mean the same thing? Does punctuation matter? Should repeating a word change the ranking, or should each unique search term count once?
strategy.proposal: Define the normalization policy explicitly, apply it consistently to the query and stored searchable text, then use unique normalized terms when the scoring contract treats repetition as irrelevant.
caveats: Deduplication intentionally loses frequency and order. It is unsuitable when those carry meaning.
Lowercasing and simple letter/digit splitting are limited text analysis. Languages, accents and stemming need explicit decisions.

If the term is in title_terms, add 3 to score. Independently, if it is in body_terms, add 1. Use two if checks, not if/elif.

decisions.lead_in: One way to compare documents is to award points for matching query words. You can award different amounts for a title match and a body match; those amounts are the scoring weights. The exercise fixes them at 3 and 1. On a new project, you would need to choose and evaluate them.

problem.title: Which document is the better match?
problem.problem: A search box can find matching documents, but it still needs an order in which to show them. A match in a title may be a stronger clue than a match buried in the body. Build a small, explainable starting point for comparing results.
reasoning: For the query “lease”, document A has “lease” in its title but not its body. Document B has it only in its body.
Under this exercise’s weights, A earns 3 and B earns 1. That makes the title match rank first, and you can explain exactly why.
Now try queries where the body-only match is actually more useful. Those examples tell you whether to change the weights or matching rules in a real product.

strategy.name: Weighted feature scoring
strategy.mechanism: Combine simple signals into a numerical score. Here, title and body matches are two independent signals with fixed weights.
strategy.use_case: A first search prototype needs explainable ranking before introducing a database text index or separate search service. Product matching and rule-based prioritization can also start from weighted signals.
strategy.prompt: “How would you rank search results for a small document collection, and know whether the ranking is useful?”
strategy.recognize: What makes a document useful for this query? Should a title match count more than a body match? Can you collect a few queries with expected results to check whether the scoring works?

problem.problem: Several firms use one document service. A document can be shared with everyone in its firm or only selected users. The service must decide whether a particular user can read it without exposing another firm’s records.

strategy.mechanism: Separate customer isolation from permissions inside that customer. Both checks must pass before content becomes accessible.

strategy.prompt: “How would you ensure users never see another customer’s documents, including through search?”

scenario.prompt: The caller can restrict search to selected categories. An omitted filter and an empty selection have different meanings.

An empty collection matches nothing.
For a nonempty collection, any shared label is enough. Labels are case-sensitive.
scenario.deliverable: Return whether a document passes the category filter.

implementation.state: Keep the requested categories separate from the document’s assigned category set.
steps: If categories is None, return True: the caller did not request a category restriction.
If a set was supplied, compare each requested category against document.categories. Return True on the first exact shared label.
If none match, return False. An empty requested set performs no successful membership checks and therefore matches nothing.

decisions.question: What does an empty category selection mean?

branches.action: Distinguish it from None; do not use a truthiness check to accept both.
Document that different API contract and handle the empty set as an unrestricted query. Update tests and callers consistently.

decisions.lead_in: The caller can omit the category filter, send an empty collection, or send particular labels. These are three different inputs. This exercise deliberately gives the first two different meanings: omission leaves results unrestricted by category, while an empty collection matches nothing.

problem.title: What does an empty selection mean?
problem.problem: A search form can request particular document categories, but the API also accepts a request with no category filter. If an empty selection and an omitted filter are treated identically, the service may return records the caller did not request.
reasoning: Compare three requests: categories=None, categories=frozenset(), and categories={“memo”}. Ask the caller what each request should mean.
For this exercise they mean: do not restrict by category; return no category matches; and accept documents labeled “memo”, respectively.
A check such as “if not categories” merges the first two requests because both are falsey in Python. Check for None explicitly before comparing labels.

strategy.name: Explicit optional-filter semantics
strategy.mechanism: Represent an omitted filter separately from a filter with zero allowed values. Evaluate set overlap only after deciding what each input state means.
strategy.use_case: Search and permission APIs often distinguish “use all categories” from “the user selected no categories”. Collapsing these states can broaden a query unexpectedly.
strategy.prompt: “An empty filter sometimes returns every record. How would you define and implement this API?”
strategy.recognize: What should happen when the filter is omitted? What if the caller supplies an empty list of labels? For several labels, must a document match any one of them or all of them?
strategy.proposal: Document the three states, validate at the API boundary, and preserve them through the query layer. Use any shared category only if the contract defines OR matching.
caveats: Some products intentionally treat an empty selection as no restriction. This exercise’s rule is not universal; agree on the contract.
Case normalization, unknown labels and AND-versus-OR semantics are separate decisions. A set alone does not settle them.

strategy.name: Filter before ranking and limiting
strategy.mechanism: Remove records the user cannot access, rank the readable matches, then take the requested page. Limiting an unfiltered ranking can discard results that should have filled the page.
strategy.use_case: Search results must fill available slots with readable matches. The same ordering issue appears in filtered product catalogs and ranked feeds.
strategy.prompt: “Our search returns two results although ten readable matches exist and the page size is ten. Where could that happen?”
strategy.recognize: When does the code check permissions: before or after choosing the page? Can the search backend filter by access before taking its top results? Are there enough readable matches to fill the requested page?

caveats: Fetching an arbitrarily larger batch and filtering afterward is a guess; it can still underfill the page or miss the best readable results.

lessons.concept:
## Help someone find a document

Someone types `termination notice` into a search box to find documents about ending an agreement. That text is the **query**: what the person is looking for. A **document** is one saved record with a title and a body (its main text).

A search engine needs a way to decide which documents to show first. In this exercise, a **score** is a number of points for matching query words. Later, you will sort documents from highest to lowest score. That ordering is called **ranking**. Today, you only calculate the number for one document.

## 1. Turn text into comparable words

A **token** is one piece of text we compare. Here, tokens are runs of letters a–z or digits 0–9. **Tokenization** means splitting text into those pieces. The provided `terms()` helper lowercases the text, splits at punctuation and spaces, and removes duplicates.

For example, `terms("NOTICE notice!")` produces `{"notice"}`. This is a Python **set**: a collection of unique values. Sets have no meaningful order. A **query term** is one of the tokens from the query.

We compare whole tokens: `notice` matches `NOTICE!` after tokenization, but does not match `notices` or `noticed`. This small practice rule does not understand meaning or synonyms.

## 2. Give each matching term points

For each distinct query term, add **3 points if it appears in the title** and **1 point if it appears in the body**. Check both places: a term in both earns 4 points. A missing term adds 0.

We chose 3 and 1 to make a title match count more than a body match. These are fixed weights for this exercise, not a universal search formula. Repeating a word in the query, title or body adds no extra points. One matching query term is enough to earn points; the document does not need to contain them all.

problem.problem: A document search worked when the archive was small. After the archive grew, request traces showed the same work on every search: open each document, split its title and body into words, and test those words against the query. reasoning: Start with document d1 in customer account firm-a: title “Lease notice”, body “Notice period”. The earlier search opens this document and checks its words on every request. We can save the result of those word checks when the document arrives.

Store one row for each distinct word, identifying the document containing it and the points that word would contribute to a search. That row is called a posting. The supplied postings table has four columns: tenant_id, term, unit_id and weight. The term column stores the word itself, such as “notice”. No separate word-ID table is needed.

First insert d1 into the supplied units table. Suppose SQLite assigns units.id = 7. The source document_id is still “d1”; 7 is the database key used to connect its rows across tables. A SearchUnit is the record you receive in Python. Here it represents a whole document, with chunk_id = "". Later, one unit can represent a smaller section, also called a chunk, of a document.

The scoring rule awards 3 points if a word appears in the title and 1 if it appears in the body. For d1, save (“firm-a”, “lease”, 7, 3), (“firm-a”, “notice”, 7, 4) and (“firm-a”, “period”, 7, 1). The last number is that word’s score contribution: notice gets 3 + 1 because it appears in both fields. It is neither a word position nor an occurrence count. Repeating notice in the body would leave its weight at 4.

Suppose a second public document d2 in firm-a has title “Schedule” and body “Period”, and receives units.id = 8. It adds (“firm-a”, “schedule”, 8, 3) and (“firm-a”, “period”, 8, 1). There are now two rows for period, one per document. This is an inverted index: a lookup starts with a word and finds the documents that contain it.

## Read the query as a pipeline
`WHERE` chooses tenant/term matches and permitted units. `GROUP BY` unit ID gathers their contributions; `SUM(weight)` computes a score. `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` choose the returned page.

```sql
SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM payments
WHERE currency = ?
GROUP BY account_id
ORDER BY total DESC, account_id ASC
LIMIT ?
```

## What SQLite supplies
FTS5 creates a searchable virtual table: `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE articles USING fts5(...)`. Write article text using INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE; FTS5 maintains its internal word lookup. Normal startup reopens the existing database.

## A prepared search expression
`make_match_query('Reset, password!')` returns `'"reset" AND "password"'`. The helper handles the FTS query syntax, while `execute(sql, parameters)` handles SQL parameter binding. They solve different problems.

## Ranking
The hidden `rank` column defaults to BM25. It accounts for word frequency, word rarity and article length. SQLite makes better matches numerically smaller. `ORDER BY rank ASC` therefore returns better matches first. This lesson uses the default formula; it does not ask you to derive or tune it.

## Follow-up interview discussion
If searches must match the exact phrase, change the query policy. If a customer reports missing useful articles, first examine sample queries and the matching/tokenization rules before changing infrastructure. If article edits do not appear, check which database is being queried and when the transaction commits.

## Iterator mechanics
A function containing `yield` returns an iterator. The caller pulls the next value with `next()` or a `for` loop. Locals remain available between yields.

```python
# Related example: consume matched spans without allocating a full split list.
for match in re.finditer(r"\S+", text):
```

Here a word is a whitespace-delimited span, unlike the lowercased letter/digit tokens used for scoring. Chunk text preserves case and punctuation; indexing later applies `terms()`.

reasoning: The store records that document d was deleted at source version 8. A retry delivers an update for d at version 6.
If deleting d also erased version 8, the update would appear to be a new document. Instead, retain “d: deleted at v8” even though its content is gone.
Compare 6 with 8 and ignore the update. A later event at version 9 is newer and can change the state. The version comparison and write must be atomic with concurrent workers.

strategy.name: Reject stale updates and retain deletion markers
strategy.mechanism: Compare the source-assigned revision before changing state. Keep the revision of a deletion in a small marker, often called a tombstone, so an older update cannot recreate the deleted document.
strategy.use_case: A webhook or change stream can deliver updates late or more than once. Without a stored revision check, an old update can overwrite newer content or restore a document that was already deleted.
strategy.prompt: “A deleted record reappears after a queue retry. How would you prevent that?”
strategy.recognize: Does the source assign a newer version number to every change of the same document? Can messages arrive twice or out of order? What remains in storage after deletion, and can two workers update it at once?
strategy.proposal: Store the latest source revision for each customer and document, including deletion markers. Apply a newer change and its revision in one database operation, ignore older changes, and report same-revision events whose content conflicts.
caveats: A read followed by a separate write can race with another worker. The database must compare and update as one atomic operation.
Versions from different independent writers may not be comparable. A timestamp alone does not necessarily provide reliable ordering.
Removing deletion markers too soon allows a very late update to recreate deleted data. Retention must account for the maximum replay or delivery delay.

branches.action: Await it directly so other tasks can run while it waits.
Run the blocking call in a worker thread with asyncio.to_thread, or replace the dependency with an async client. Cancelling the await does not forcibly stop an already-running thread.

decisions.lead_in: The lookup function calls a dependency, such as a database or HTTP client. An async-native dependency lets the event loop run other tasks while it waits. A blocking dependency occupies the event-loop thread until it returns, even when called from an async function.

problem.title: An async endpoint is slow and shares request state
problem.problem: A batch endpoint takes roughly one lookup duration per item despite being declared async. A helper also returns tags left behind by previous calls. These symptoms need separate explanations.
reasoning: Five independent lookups each wait about 100 ms. Awaiting them one by one takes roughly 500 ms; overlapping their waits can bring the total closer to one lookup’s duration.

But time.sleep() inside the async function blocks the event-loop thread. Use an async wait for the fake. For a real dependency that only offers a blocking call, run that call in a worker thread with asyncio.to_thread.
Separately, replace a default tags=[] with per-call list creation. Calling the helper for “a”, then “b”, should produce [“a”] and [“b”], not accumulate both.

strategy.name: Cooperative concurrency and isolated call state
strategy.mechanism: Let independent I/O overlap without blocking the event loop, and ensure each function call owns its mutable state.
strategy.use_case: A batch handler serializes lookups and accumulates tags from earlier requests, causing latency and cross-request state leakage.
strategy.prompt: “This async endpoint gets slower under load, and one request sees another request’s tags. How would you investigate?”

strategy.proposal: Use per-call state, schedule independent lookups concurrently and use an async client; if the dependency only provides a blocking call, run that call in a worker thread with asyncio.to_thread. Preserve ordered results and explicit failure behavior.
caveats: Moving work to threads does not make cancellation forcibly stop that work.

from __future__ import annotations

import time


# This file is intentionally bad.
# Your task is to improve it while preserving the externally tested behavior.


async def expensive_lookup(item_id: str) -> str:
    """
    Pretend this is a blocking legacy SDK call.

    BUG:
    `time.sleep()` blocks the entire asyncio event loop.
    Refactor so multiple calls can make progress concurrently.

    You are allowed to:
    - introduce a synchronous helper and use asyncio.to_thread(), OR
    - replace the fake with an async equivalent for this exercise.

    In an interview, explain what you would do if the real dependency were a
    blocking DB/HTTP library versus an async-native library.
    """
    time.sleep(0.10)
    return item_id.upper()


def add_audit_tag(tag: str, tags: list[str] = []):
    """
    BUG:
    mutable default argument leaks state across calls.

    Preserve behavior:
        add_audit_tag("a") -> ["a"]
        add_audit_tag("b") -> ["b"]

    Do not make callers responsible for passing [].
    """
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags


async def process_items(item_ids: list[str]) -> list[str | None]:
    """
    Process all items concurrently.

    Requirements
    ------------
    1. Preserve input order.
    2. Run lookups concurrently.
    3. If one lookup raises a normal Exception, put None in that position.
    4. Do NOT swallow asyncio.CancelledError.
    5. The normal happy path for 5 items should take roughly one lookup duration,
       not five lookup durations.

    The starter implementation is intentionally naive.
    """
    results: list[str | None] = []
    for item_id in item_ids:
        try:
            results.append(await expensive_lookup(item_id))
        except Exception:
            results.append(None)
    return results

lessons.contract:
Exercise 1: bounded concurrent document fetching.

Requirements
------------
1. Fetch documents concurrently.
2. Never have more than `max_concurrency` fetcher calls in flight.
3. Apply `timeout_s` independently to each fetch.
4. A timeout/error for one ID must produce None for that position,
   not fail the whole batch.
5. Preserve the exact input order.
6. Duplicate IDs must only trigger ONE downstream fetch, while still
   appearing multiple times in the returned list.
7. Empty input should return [].

Constraints
-----------
- Use asyncio; do not use threads.
- Keep the public function signature unchanged.

Interview follow-ups to answer after you pass the tests
--------------------------------------------------------
- What happens if `ids` contains 500,000 IDs?
- Does a semaphore alone prevent creating 500,000 tasks?
- How would you implement global concurrency limits across 20 processes?
- Would you retry all failures? Which ones? With what backoff?
- If the caller is cancelled, what should happen to child work?

problem.title: Why is work still running after the request ends?
problem.problem: A user leaves a search page while several backend lookups are running. The request is no longer needed, but its child tasks continue consuming connections and source capacity. Decide who should stop and clean up that work.
reasoning: A request starts tasks A and B. The user closes the page while both tasks are waiting on backend calls.
The parent request receives cancellation. It asks A and B to stop, then waits for their cleanup so connections are released.
Let cancellation reach the caller. Returning [] would falsely describe this as a completed search with no matches.

strategy.name: Cancellation propagation and owned cleanup
strategy.mechanism: Treat cancellation as a request to stop an operation, propagate it through child work, and wait for cleanup before the parent finishes.
strategy.use_case: One request starts several downstream searches. If the client disconnects or its deadline expires, those child calls should stop because no caller will use their results.
strategy.prompt: “Requests disappear, but their background lookups keep consuming connections. What would you change?”
strategy.recognize: Which lookups belong to this request? Who receives the cancellation when the user leaves? Do child tasks release their connections before the parent finishes?
strategy.proposal: Give child tasks a clear lifetime tied to the request. On cancellation, cancel and await those children, use finally for resource cleanup, and let cancellation reach the caller.
caveats: Cancellation is cooperative. Blocking calls or dependencies that ignore cancellation may keep running.

problem.title: One search depends on several unreliable backends
problem.problem: A search request queries several repositories. Calling them one by one is slow, but starting unlimited calls can overload dependencies. A failure in one repository should not discard useful matches from the others.
reasoning: Repositories A and B usually answer in 100 ms and 200 ms. Start them together rather than waiting for A before starting B.
If there are more repositories than available call slots, leave the extra calls waiting. Start each call’s timeout only when it gets a slot, as this exercise requires.
If A succeeds and B times out, return A’s hits and report B as failed. Do not pretend B completed and found zero matches.

lessons.contract:
Exercise 3: idempotent document ingestion.

Identity
--------
A document is uniquely identified by:
    (tenant_id, external_id)

Requirements
------------
1. First ingestion creates the document with version=1.
2. Re-ingesting identical content/source is a no-op:
   version must NOT increase.
3. If content OR source changes, update the existing document and increment
   version by exactly 1.
4. Same external_id in different tenants represents two independent docs.
5. If the same identity appears multiple times in one input batch, process
   it in input order. The final stored state should reflect the final item.

Keep it simple. This is an in-memory exercise.

Interview follow-ups
--------------------
- Translate this to PostgreSQL. What UNIQUE constraint would you use?
- Would SELECT-then-INSERT be race safe?
- How would INSERT ... ON CONFLICT help?
- Where would you draw the transaction boundary for a batch?
- If ingestion triggers embedding/indexing, how would you make that side
  effect idempotent too?
- What happens when two workers ingest updates concurrently?

    external_id: str
    content: str
    source: str


@dataclass
class StoredDocument:
    tenant_id: str
    external_id: str
    content: str
    source: str
    version: int


class InMemoryDocumentStore:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        # You may change the internal representation.
        self._documents: dict[tuple[str, str], StoredDocument] = {}

    def get(self, tenant_id: str, external_id: str) -> StoredDocument | None:

    def all(self) -> list[StoredDocument]:

scenario.prompt: Search works on a small collection but misses its latency target at millions of documents. How would you scale it?
requirements: Preserve tenant and document permissions.
Account for index and cache freshness, including access revocation.
State workload assumptions and how you would measure the change.
scenario.deliverable: Propose the retrieval design and explain its trade-offs.

implementation.state: Define the indexed fields, trusted access filters, stable sort fields, page cursor and freshness target.
steps: Measure the existing request path. For text lookup, consider an inverted index mapping terms to document IDs so a query need not scan every document.
Submit query and eligibility filters together to candidate retrieval. Rank eligible matches and return a stable page with a defined tie-break.
Load permitted result fields and propagate version/access changes to the index and caches. Recheck access when the freshness policy requires it.
Test relevance examples alongside latency, and test revocation while a cached result exists.
implementation.result: A design that names where lookup, authorization, pagination and update handling execute.

decisions.question: Can the index be temporarily stale?

branches.action: Measure that lag and make the user-visible behavior explicit. Sensitive access changes may still need a fresher check.
Add an authoritative permission check or stronger invalidation path before exposing content; do not rely solely on an eventually updated index.

decisions.lead_in: An index is a searchable copy of information from the document store. A change in the store may reach the index later, leaving the index temporarily stale. That delay is especially important when the changed information is whether a user may read a document.

connections.text: Use the actual SQLite plan and bounded-result exercise as the starting point for a scale discussion. It is not a million-document load test.

problem.title: Search slows down as the collection grows
problem.problem: The local search is correct on a small collection, but scanning millions of documents no longer meets the response-time target. Some records also change permissions while search data is cached or indexed.
reasoning: A request currently reads every document to find the word “lease”. Measure how much time is spent scanning, ranking and loading result content.
An index can record which documents contain “lease”, reducing how many records the request must examine. Customer and permission restrictions still apply.
If a user loses access while a cached search result exists, decide how that result is invalidated or rechecked. A faster lookup must not preserve outdated access.

strategy.name: Indexed retrieval with scoped candidates
strategy.mechanism: Use a text index to find likely matches without reading every document. Apply customer and permission rules before limiting, and give equal scores a stable order.
strategy.use_case: A shared knowledge service has grown until reading every document inside each application request misses its response-time or memory target.
strategy.prompt: “Search is fast with ten thousand documents but too slow with ten million. What changes?”
strategy.recognize: How long do scanning, ranking and loading results each take? How often do documents and permissions change? How quickly must an update or access revocation affect search?
strategy.proposal: Choose a database text index or search service that fits the query workload, apply customer and permission constraints while finding matches, and keep pagination and cached results inside the same customer and permission scope. Compare latency and relevance before and after.
caveats: An index is derived data and can lag behind source changes. Permission revocations and deletions need an explicit freshness policy.
A faster search that changes eligibility or relevance is not automatically correct. Measure both system performance and user-facing quality.

brief.heading: Move beyond scanning every document
brief.scenario: Your working search scans a local collection. Discuss how to serve many more documents while preserving access rules.

vocabulary.meaning: A data structure that helps locate candidates without scanning every document.
The best K eligible matches, where K is the requested limit.
Stored results reused to avoid repeated work.
Time from a request to its response.

brief.rule: State your workload assumptions. Explain how ranking and permission changes remain correct as retrieval and caching move into other components.
brief.example: If a user loses access after a result is cached, the next response must respect the changed permission.

lessons.title: Search slows down as the collection grows
lessons.summary: The local search is correct on a small collection, but scanning millions of documents no longer meets the response-time target.
lessons.question: Your local scan works. Now design the next step for millions of documents while preserving permissions.
criteria: States workload and latency assumptions before choosing infrastructure
Moves candidate filtering/ranking to an appropriate retrieval layer
Explains permission updates, caches and top-K correctness
Names a measurement and one deliberate trade-off
lessons.guide: Start from the current invariant: return the best eligible results. Discuss what moves into the retrieval engine, what must not be loaded per request, and how permission changes affect indexes/cache keys. There is no mandatory infrastructure vendor. Counts and caches can leak information even when document bodies are filtered.
followups: What happens immediately after access is revoked?
How would you know the index rather than I/O is the bottleneck?

scenario.prompt: A document is saved, but a crash prevents its indexing job from being sent. Design a path that can recover.
requirements: The main store and searchable view can temporarily disagree.
Jobs may repeat, arrive late or fail.
Carry document identity and version through downstream work, including deletions.
scenario.deliverable: Explain component responsibilities, failure recovery and stale-write protection.

implementation.state: Store authoritative document revision plus durable pending indexing work; carry identity and revision in every job.
steps: In one database transaction, apply the validated revision change and write an outbox/work record for it.
A relay reads pending work, publishes it, and records progress with a retry-safe policy. Publication may repeat after a crash.
A worker extracts the text and sends its source version to the search store. That store atomically compares versions and applies the change, retaining the version for a deletion too.
Track retries and failed jobs explicitly, and include deletion events in the same derived-store update path.
implementation.result: After a crash, unfinished work can be found and replayed without pretending duplicate delivery is impossible.

decisions.question: Can you atomically commit state and the work record?

branches.action: A transactional outbox can close the save-versus-notify gap within that store.
Define an explicit reconciliation or replay mechanism that detects missing derived updates. Two independent best-effort writes do not guarantee recovery.

decisions.lead_in: A possible recovery design is to save a pending work record alongside the document update, saying that this version still needs indexing. To commit them atomically means the database saves both or saves neither. A worker or relay can later read the pending record and arrange the indexing.

problem.title: The document was saved but never became searchable
problem.problem: A document update reaches the main store, then the process crashes before notifying the indexing worker. The stored record and the searchable view disagree, and a simple retry might repeat work already done.
reasoning: Save document d at version 5, then imagine a crash immediately before publishing its indexing job. The database now has v5 but search does not.
One option is to save an indexing-work record in the same transaction as d. After a restart, a relay can find and publish that unfinished work.

The relay might publish twice, so identical repeats must have no additional effect. If a v5 worker pauses while v6 is applied, the search store must atomically reject the later v5 write. Checking the source version before writing leaves a race.

strategy.name: Recoverable background indexing
strategy.mechanism: Store each accepted document change, then use retryable background work to update searchable copies. At the search store, atomically accept only newer document versions, so delayed workers cannot replace newer data.
strategy.use_case: A connector updates a document store and triggers extraction, chunking and search indexing across separate components.
strategy.prompt: “The database update succeeds, but the indexing job is never sent. How do we recover?”
strategy.recognize: Which store is authoritative? What if the process crashes between saving a change and sending a job? Can a job run twice, and how will a slow worker detect that its document has changed?
strategy.proposal: One option is a transactional outbox: save the document change and a pending-work row in the same database transaction. A relay sends that work to the queue. Workers may receive it more than once, so repeating a completed job must have no additional effect, and the search store compares the incoming version and writes in one atomic operation. Retain the version when deleting too, so an older job cannot recreate removed text.
caveats: The pending-work row prevents a committed document change from losing its indexing request, but delivery may repeat after a crash. Workers still need safe retry behavior.
Retries need limits, observability and repair paths. A job that keeps failing must not silently block all later work.
Deletion and permission changes must reach every derived store, including caches and embeddings.

brief.heading: Follow a document from source to search
brief.scenario: Design how imported changes become searchable, including what happens when a component fails partway through.

vocabulary.meaning: The component receiving or fetching source changes.
Reading document text / splitting it into text chunks.
Updating the structures used to retrieve documents.
A stored change may succeed while sending its work notification fails.

brief.rule: Explain ownership, recovery and how document identity and source version travel through each step.
brief.example: A document update is saved, then the process crashes before notifying the index worker. Your design needs a recovery path.

lessons.title: The document was saved but never became searchable
lessons.summary: A document update reaches the main store, then the process crashes before notifying the indexing worker.
lessons.question: Sketch connector → version store → extraction/chunking → indexing → query, and explain failures.
criteria: Names a source of truth and component responsibilities
Explains duplicates, retries, stale events and deletion
Closes or explicitly handles the database commit/publish gap
Carries identity/version through asynchronous work
lessons.guide: Use the V2 event semantics as a starting point, not “exactly once” as an explanation. Describe how a durable outbox or an explicit reconciliation mechanism handles committed-but-not-published updates. Use an atomic version-conditional write in the destination store, including deletion markers; reading the source version separately still allows two workers to race.
followups: Can a slow worker overwrite newer content?
How do deletions reach every derived store?

scenario.prompt: Design a documentation assistant whose answers users can verify against readable source text.
requirements: Check access before source content reaches the model.
Keep source identities through search and model-input selection.
Handle missing evidence and invalid references; source identity alone does not prove a claim.
scenario.deliverable: Describe the path from document search to answer and reference validation.

implementation.state: Keep readable retrieved chunks, the model input budget, selected source IDs and a label-to-source map.
steps: Retrieve using tenant and user scope. Select useful chunks within the remaining model budget and assign source labels only after selection.
Send the question and selected text with a clear output/reference contract. Treat retrieved content as data, not authorization or application instructions.
Validate reference labels against the selected map. Evaluate whether the cited text supports claims, separately from validating output structure.
Specify no-evidence and interrupted-generation responses, and avoid claiming support when no source was found.
implementation.result: An answer path whose access decisions, context selection and reference checks have explicit owners.

decisions.question: What if retrieval finds no useful permitted evidence?

branches.action: Return an explicit no-evidence response or ask a clarifying question; do not fabricate references.
Label that mode clearly and keep it separate from source-backed answers. Agree on this behavior rather than letting it happen silently.

decisions.lead_in: Retrieval is the search for source text relevant to the user’s question. It can return nothing useful, either because the documentation lacks the answer or because the user cannot access it. The product needs a defined response for that case before generation begins.

problem.title: Users cannot verify the assistant’s answer
problem.problem: An assistant answers questions about private, changing documentation. Users need to know which source supports an answer, and the service must avoid sending restricted information to the model.
reasoning: A user asks how to configure a feature. Retrieve readable documentation sections about that feature and keep each section’s document ID.
Select text that fits the request, label the included sections and ask for references using those labels.
If the answer cites [2], first check that [2] exists, then check whether its text supports the claim. A real ID with unrelated content is still a bad citation.

strategy.name: Retrieval-augmented generation with verifiable sources
strategy.mechanism: Search for permitted source text before calling the model, keep each section’s document ID, and check that answer references point to supplied text.
strategy.use_case: An internal documentation assistant answers questions whose facts change too often to rely only on a model’s training data.
strategy.prompt: “How would you build a document assistant whose answers users can check?”
strategy.recognize: Which documents may this user read? How do you tell whether a retrieved section answers the question? How will users open a cited source, and what happens when no useful source is found?
strategy.proposal: Search only permitted documents, choose source text that fits the model input limit, and preserve reference IDs. Require explicit handling for no evidence and unknown reference labels, then evaluate whether cited text supports each claim.
caveats: Retrieval does not guarantee correctness, and valid reference formatting is weaker than factual support.
Retrieved documents are untrusted input and may contain instructions. Keep them distinct from application instructions and enforce permissions outside the model.
More context can add noise and cost. Evaluate chunking, selection and answer quality together.

brief.heading: Keep generated answers tied to their sources
brief.scenario: A service retrieves readable text chunks and sends selected text to a model, then shows an answer with references.

vocabulary.meaning: Finding relevant source text chunks.
The text chunks supplied to help the model answer.
The record of where a text chunk or reference came from.
Whether a cited text chunk actually supports the answer’s claim.

brief.rule: Discuss access checks, selection limits and reference validation separately. A valid reference ID alone does not prove a claim.
brief.example: A reference may point to a real text chunk while the answer says something that text chunk never states.

lessons.title: Users cannot verify the assistant’s answer
lessons.summary: An assistant answers questions about private, changing documentation.
lessons.question: Design the boundary from retrieval to generated answer and references.
criteria: Checks access before content reaches the model
Keeps stable document/chunk identities through context selection
Handles no eligible context and unknown reference labels
Distinguishes provenance, schema validity and factual support
lessons.guide: The supplied context exercise preserves a reference mapping and a word budget. A production model needs its actual tokenizer/context budget and an output-evaluation approach. Reject unknown labels, but remember that a known label alone does not prove that its source supports a claim.
followups: Where do you enforce permissions before prompting?
What would you return with no eligible context?

scenario.prompt: One slow backend holds up a response even though other sources have finished. Bound the wait and define what callers receive.
requirements: Include queueing in the overall request deadline.
Distinguish a failed source from one that returned no matches.
Own cancellation and cleanup, and consider limits across service replicas.
scenario.deliverable: Propose deadlines and partial-result behavior.

implementation.state: Track an absolute operation deadline using a monotonic clock, plus each source outcome and owned task.
steps: At request start, calculate deadline = now + total_budget. Before starting/waiting for work, calculate remaining = deadline - now.
Do not begin work when remaining is exhausted. Cap source waits by the remaining request budget as well as any source-specific limit.
At expiry, cancel and await owned work, then return the allowed partial response with unfinished/failed sources identified.
Measure queue time, completed-source coverage and deadline misses; use those measurements to tune budgets.
implementation.result: Waiting for a slot cannot silently extend the request beyond its agreed lifetime.

decisions.question: Are partial results useful to the caller?

branches.action: Return successes with explicit completeness information and stop work that can no longer contribute.
Fail the operation according to the API contract when required sources cannot complete. Do not return partial data disguised as complete.

decisions.lead_in: If some sources finish and another does not, the system has a partial result: it knows some answers but not the missing source’s answer. Returning those successes may be useful for search; for an operation that requires every source, the same response could be misleading.

problem.title: One slow dependency holds up the response
problem.problem: A request combines results from several services. One becomes slow, stretching user-visible latency even when the others finish quickly. You need to decide how long to wait and what an incomplete answer should communicate.
reasoning: The whole request has a 500 ms deadline. One source spends 300 ms waiting for a slot, so giving its call another unrestricted 500 ms would exceed that deadline.
Use the remaining request time when deciding whether to start or keep waiting for work. Return successful sources if partial results are acceptable.
Tell the caller which sources did not finish. Track how often useful sources are excluded before tightening timeouts further.

strategy.name: Deadline-aware graceful degradation
strategy.mechanism: Give the whole request a deadline, divide that time among downstream calls, and state when the response omits a source that did not finish.
strategy.use_case: A user-facing search queries several systems with different response times while needing a predictable overall latency.
strategy.prompt: “How can we keep response latency bounded when one backend becomes slow?”
strategy.recognize: How long may the entire request take, including waiting for a call slot? Is a partial response useful? How should the caller distinguish a timeout from a successful source with zero results?
strategy.proposal: Set an operation deadline, account for queue time, use per-source limits within the remaining budget and cancel work that no longer serves the request. Report completeness explicitly.
caveats: Aggressive deadlines can systematically exclude a useful slow source. Monitor quality and completeness as well as speed.
Retries consume the same budget and can amplify overload. Avoid automatic retries without considering remaining time and failure type.

brief.heading: Return useful results when one source is slow
brief.scenario: A query calls several retrieval services. Discuss how to bound waiting while reporting incomplete results honestly.

vocabulary.meaning: How long one source call may run.
When the entire request must finish, including time spent waiting.
Another running copy of the service.
A response that distinguishes successful searches from missing or failed sources.

brief.rule: Account for queueing, cancellation and cleanup, and distinguish limits inside one process from limits across all replicas.
brief.example: A source returning no matches succeeded. A source that timed out leaves its matches unknown.

lessons.title: One slow dependency holds up the response
lessons.summary: A request combines results from several services.
lessons.question: Several retrieval sources have different latency and error rates. Design deadlines and partial results.
criteria: Distinguishes operation deadline from per-source timeout
Makes partial failure visible to the caller
Owns cancellation and resource cleanup
Discusses replica-level limits and useful metrics
lessons.guide: A local semaphore is not a fleet-wide limit. Explain what happens while waiting for a slot, after caller cancellation and when a source returns no hits versus fails. Measure queues, active calls, latency and failure rates before adding more capacity.
followups: Which timeout starts when a slot is acquired?
What changes across twenty processes?

scenario.prompt: The HTTP handler mixes validation, permissions, search and database access. Make the behavior reusable and testable.
requirements: Trusted identity must reach application and data-access checks.
Keep transport-specific decisions at the HTTP boundary.
Core search must be testable without starting an HTTP server.
scenario.deliverable: Explain the responsibilities, interfaces and error mapping.

implementation.state: Define a request adapter, reusable search operation and tenant-scoped repository interface.
steps: The handler validates transport inputs and resolves trusted identity. Pass simple values into the application operation.
The operation enforces reusable business behavior and calls the repository with explicit scope; the repository applies scoped queries.
Map application results/errors to HTTP response models and statuses. Add request IDs and timing at the boundary while keeping sensitive content out of routine logs.
Test core behavior with a fake repository and separately test HTTP validation, identity propagation and error mapping.
implementation.result: Other callers can reuse search behavior without invoking or copying an HTTP route.

decisions.question: Does a rule depend on HTTP?

branches.answer: Yes, such as reading a header or choosing a status code
branches.action: Keep it in the HTTP-specific boundary code.

branches.answer: No, such as deciding whether a document is readable
branches.action: Keep it in reusable application/data-access behavior so non-HTTP callers cannot bypass it.

decisions.lead_in: The handler currently mixes details of HTTP, such as headers and status codes, with rules that should also hold for a batch caller. Separating them requires deciding which behavior belongs specifically to receiving an HTTP request and which belongs to the search operation itself.

problem.title: The route handler owns too many responsibilities
problem.problem: An HTTP search handler contains validation, permissions, search rules and database calls. It is hard to test and would be difficult to reuse from a batch job without copying behavior.
reasoning: An HTTP request contains search text and caller credentials. The handler validates and translates those inputs into an application call.
The search logic decides eligibility and matching; the repository executes scoped data access. Test those rules with in-memory records without starting HTTP.
If a batch job later needs the same search, it can call that application logic with trusted scope instead of copying the HTTP handler.

strategy.name: Separation of transport, policy and storage
strategy.mechanism: Define small boundaries so HTTP translation, application decisions and data access can change and be tested independently.
strategy.use_case: A search function needs an HTTP endpoint today and may later be called from a batch job or another transport.
strategy.prompt: “Where would you put validation, authorization and database code in this service?”
strategy.recognize: Which rules depend on HTTP and which must hold for every caller? Who verifies identity? Can you test document permissions and search behavior without starting a server?
strategy.proposal: Translate and validate requests at the edge, enforce business and access rules in reusable logic and pass the verified customer scope into the database query. Map errors to HTTP without leaking internal details.
caveats: More layers do not necessarily improve the design. Add a boundary when it isolates a real responsibility or source of change.
Duplicated policy logic can drift. Make ownership explicit and test bypass paths, not just the happy-path endpoint.

brief.heading: Separate HTTP from search behavior
brief.scenario: Turn a working search function into a service that clients can call, with clear boundaries for validation and storage.

vocabulary.meaning: The function translating an HTTP request into an application call.
The interface used to access stored documents.
Verifying who the caller is / deciding what they may access.
Logs, timing and traces connected to one request.

brief.rule: Keep core search testable without HTTP. Explain where trusted identity, validation and error translation belong.
brief.example: The same search behavior should be testable using in-memory documents without starting a web server.

lessons.title: The route handler owns too many responsibilities
lessons.summary: An HTTP search handler contains validation, permissions, search rules and database calls.
lessons.question: Wrap your search function in an API without mixing every concern into the route.
criteria: Separates validation/transport from application logic and storage
Uses trusted authenticated identity rather than an arbitrary tenant header
Describes error semantics and request-scoped observability
Keeps the core function testable without HTTP
lessons.guide: FastAPI is an adapter, not the architecture itself. The original header-based exercise deliberately fakes trusted identity. Discuss authentication, authorization and query-layer enforcement separately. Prefer small testable boundaries over a speculative framework.
followups: Can the user choose a tenant just by sending a header?
What is an integration test versus a unit test here?
